leach1998.title: UUIDs and GUIDs (IETF Internet-Draft draft-leach-uuids-guids-01)
leach1998.author: Paul J. Leach (Microsoft), Rich Salz (Certco)
leach1998.quote: One of the main reasons for using UUIDs is that no centralized authority is required to administer them (beyond the one that allocates IEEE 802.1 node identifiers). As a result, generation on demand can be completely automated, and they can be used for a wide variety of purposes. The UUID generation algorithm described here supports very high allocation rates: 10 million per second per machine if you need it, so that they could even be used as transaction IDs.
supports: the parenthesis that names the borrowed coordination
February 1998 date of the draft
node field is the IEEE address: 'For UUID version 1, the node field consists of the IEEE address, usually the host address.'
clock sequence rationale: 'For UUID version 1, the clock sequence is used to help avoid duplicates that could arise when the clock is set backwards in time or if the node ID changes.'
security considerations: 'It should not be assumed that UUIDs are hard to guess; they should not be used as capabilities.'

rfc4122.title: RFC 4122: A Universally Unique IDentifier (UUID) URN Namespace
rfc4122.author: P. Leach, M. Mealling, R. Salz
rfc4122.quote: For UUID version 1, the node field consists of an IEEE 802 MAC address, usually the host address.  For systems with multiple IEEE 802 addresses, any available one can be used.
supports: v1 node field is the MAC address, restated in the standards-track RFC

S4.5 'Node IDs that Do Not Identify the Host': 'One approach is to contact the IEEE and get a separate block of addresses.  At the time of writing, the application could be found at <http://standards.ieee.org/regauth/oui/pilot-ind.html>, and the cost was US$550.'
S6 Security Considerations: 'Do not assume that UUIDs are hard to guess; they should not be used as security capabilities (identifiers whose mere possession grants access), for example.'

rfc9562.title: RFC 9562: Universally Unique IDentifiers (UUIDs)
rfc9562.author: K. Davis, B. Peabody, P. Leach
rfc9562.quote: MAC addresses pose inherent security risks around privacy and SHOULD NOT be used within a UUID.  Instead CSPRNG data SHOULD be selected from a source with sufficient entropy to ensure guaranteed uniqueness among UUID generation.
supports: May 2024 publication, Obsoletes: 4122

the reason RFC 4122 was replaced, item 4: 'Privacy and network security issues arise from using a Media Access Control (MAC) address in the node field of UUIDv1.  Exposed MAC addresses can be used as an attack surface to locate network interfaces and reveal various other information about such machines'
UUIDv7: 'UUIDv7 values are created by allocating a Unix timestamp in milliseconds in the most significant 48 bits'

the timestamp's own cost: 'Timestamps embedded in the UUID do pose a very small attack surface.  The timestamp in conjunction with an embedded counter does signal the order of creation for a given UUID and its corresponding data'

UUIDs were 'originally used in the Apollo Network Computing System (NCS), later in the Open Software Foundation's (OSF's) Distributed Computing Environment (DCE), and then in Microsoft Windows platforms.'

UUIDv4's random budget, S5.4: an implementation 'MAY choose to randomly generate the exact required number of bits for random_a, random_b, and random_c (122 bits total)' -- 122 random bits, not 128, because ver and var are fixed
UUIDv7 puts the timestamp in the LEADING 48 bits (S5.7 figure: unix_ts_ms, ver, rand_a, var, rand_b); the trailing bits where UUIDv1 kept the MAC are random in v7

'The investigator, Richard Smith, 45, is the president of Phar Lap Software, a small software development company here.'
'he was the one who this month raised questions about the propriety of a little-known Microsoft feature that embeds unique hardware numbers in every Microsoft Office document file.'

gao1999.author: Keith A. Rhodes, U.S. General Accounting Office
gao1999.quote: According to the CERT Coordination Center, the first confirmed reports of the virus were received on Friday, March 26, 1999. By Monday, March 29, it had reached more than 100,000 computers at more than 300 organizations.
supports: the Melissa date and the Monday spread figure
'Second, Melissa showed how hard it is to trace any virus back to its source. At first, it was widely assumed that Melissa was created by a writer, known by the computer handle VicodinES'

GAO explicitly declined to price it: 'there are no data available at this time that quantify the impact of the virus, for example, productivity lost or the value of data lost.' The $80m figure is therefore NOT from GAO -- it is from the federal plea agreement, cited separately as doj2002.

msoffice97.title: Microsoft, Office 97, and Privacy (Office Update)
msoffice97.author: Yusuf Mehdi, Director of Windows Marketing, Microsoft Corporation
msoffice97.quote: The unique indentifier generated for Office 97 documents contains information that is derived in part from a network card, not from an individual user's identity, and thus it is not possible to reliably determine the author of a document. The unique identifier number has not been widely used by third parties and in light of customer privacy concerns, Microsoft has decided to help customers remove the identifier.
supports: the two downloads by name: 'Microsoft Office 97 Unique Identifier Patch' ('once applied will prevent the insertion of a unique identifier number in all new Office documents') and 'Microsoft Office 97 Unique Identifier Removal Tool'
'The forthcoming release of Office 2000 will not include the ability to insert unique identifier numbers in documents.'
page carries no publication date; footer reads (c) 1999 Microsoft Corporation. Read from the Internet Archive capture of 1999-11-27. 'indentifier' is Microsoft's typo, quoted as it appears.

smith97.title: Fingerprinting of Office 97 files (computerbytesman.com)
smith97.author: Richard M. Smith
smith97.quote: In Office 97, when an Word, Excel, or PowerPoint file is saved for the first time, it is assigned its own unique serial number. This serial number is the form a 32-digit GUID (Globally Unique ID). The last 12 digits of a GUID will most likely contain the MAC or NIC address of Ethernet adapter of the person saving the document.
supports: 'The GUID serial numnber was originally put in Office 97 document files to correct broken hyperlinks. Ironically this feature was never implemented, but the serial numbers remain.'
'To locate a GUID in a Word document, simply open the .DOC file in Notepad and search for the string "GUID".'
smith97.note: Smith's own page, but undated: the earliest Internet Archive capture is 2001-12-01, so `year` records the capture, not the writing. Typos ('an Word', 'numnber') are his, quoted as they appear. Nothing dated 1999 is claimed from this source.

unverified: That Smith's March 1999 Office 97 disclosure and his Melissa fingerprinting used the same published technique: the NYT reports both facts about the same person in the same article but does not state the method was identical.
The exact publication date of Richard M. Smith's computerbytesman.com 'Fingerprinting of Office 97 files' page; the earliest capture is 2001-12-01 and the page itself is undated.

Whether the GUID evidence, rather than the America Online account tip, is what identified David L. Smith. The DOJ release says the arrest 'followed a tip from a representative of America Online', and GAO says that without AOL's cooperation 'the suspect might not have ever been identified' -- GAO also records that the VicodinES attribution was the initial, widely held assumption and that the AOL account used was stolen. The story therefore claims only that Richard Smith gave the FBI a lead.
The exact 1999 release date of the Microsoft Office 97 Unique Identifier Patch; the Office Update letter announcing it carries no date beyond a 1999 copyright line.

The $80 million figure as a GAO number. GAO's April 1999 testimony says the opposite -- that no data quantifying the impact were available. The figure is the defendant's own plea-agreement acknowledgement, and is cited to DOJ.
